title: Out of Africa dispersal of Homo sapiens
summary: Between roughly 70,000 and 45,000 years ago, a population of Homo sapiens left Africa and spread across Eurasia to Australia; nearly all ancestry of people living outside Africa today traces back to it.
card: Genomes of living people show that almost everyone outside Africa descends mainly from one population that left the continent after a bottleneck, which genetic studies date to between about 72,000 and 50,000 years ago. Its members interbred with Neanderthals about 50,500–43,500 years ago and, in the ancestry of Papuans and Aboriginal Australians, with Denisovans. Earlier exits, such as the one recorded at Misliya Cave in Israel, left little trace, and the route and the date of arrival in Australia are still argued.
what:
Out of Africa refers to the dispersal of Homo sapiens from Africa into Eurasia and on to Sahul, the Pleistocene landmass joining Australia and New Guinea. Genomes of present-day people show that nearly all ancestry outside Africa traces to one founding population that left the continent and passed through a population bottleneck. Malaspinas and colleagues (2016) dated that bottleneck to about 72,000 years ago (95% interval 60,000–104,000) and the split of the ancestors of Aboriginal Australians and Papuans from Eurasians to about 58,000 years ago (51,000–72,000), assuming a mutation rate of 1.25 × 10⁻⁸ per site per generation and 29-year generations; other genetic studies reviewed by López and colleagues (2015) give 60,000–50,000 years. A firm minimum comes from Neanderthal DNA: most of it in non-Africans entered during one extended period of interbreeding about 50,500–43,500 years ago, so the founding population had left Africa by then and was still largely a single group.

It was not the first exit. A maxilla from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel, is dated to 177,000–194,000 years ago; Homo sapiens remains from Skhul and Qafzeh in the same region to roughly 90,000–120,000 years ago; and a partial skull from Apidima Cave in southern Greece to more than 210,000 years ago, an identification and date that other researchers dispute. Genetic results imply that such early groups were not the main ancestors of living non-Africans, although some models allow them a small share.

Scholars still disagree on the route, the number of waves and the date people reached Australia. Genetic studies have been read as favouring either a southern crossing of the Bab el-Mandeb strait into Arabia or a northern exit through Egypt and Sinai, and a date of about 65,000 years for first occupation at Madjedbebe in northern Australia conflicts with arguments for arrival nearer 50,000 years ago. By about 45,000 years ago, descendants of the dispersal were living from central Europe to western Siberia, and Sahul had been settled.

uncertainty.note: Start: genetic estimates for the founding bottleneck and exit range from ~72 ka (95% CI 60–104 ka; Malaspinas et al. 2016) to 60–50 ka (studies reviewed by López et al. 2015; 50–55 ka preferred by O'Connell et al. 2018); all depend on assumed mutation rates and generation times. End: by ~45 ka H. sapiens of this lineage were at Ust'-Ishim (46,880–43,210 cal BP) and Ranis (43,400–46,580 cal BP), and Sahul was settled by 47.5–55 ka. Earlier dispersals (Apidima >210 ka, Misliya 177–194 ka, Skhul/Qafzeh ~90–120 ka) are outside this span by design. Years are counted back from the present; the 1950 vs 2026 reference difference is negligible at this precision.

where.modern_name: Bab el-Mandeb strait between Djibouti and Eritrea and Yemen (representative pin for the candidate southern exit; the northern alternative runs through Egypt and Sinai)
where.historical_name: Strait between the Horn of Africa and southwestern Arabia; no recorded place names or polities exist at this date. Pleistocene sea level stood well below today's at times (about 100 m lower at the maximum Late Pleistocene regression, ~120 m at the Last Glacial Maximum), exposing the Sunda and Sahul shelves, while Wallacea always required sea crossings.

how: The dispersal was a slow spread of small foraging groups over thousands of years, not a planned migration. (1) Climate opened and closed corridors: Groucutt and colleagues link expansions to humid phases, in Marine Isotope Stage 5 (~125–75 ka) and again in Stage 3 (~55–45 ka), when parts of Arabia turned to grassland and savanna. (2) Lower sea levels, about 100 m below today at the deepest Late Pleistocene regression, narrowed water gaps and exposed the Sunda and Sahul shelves, but Wallacea was never joined to either, so reaching Sahul needed open-sea voyages along island routes of 1,000–1,500 km, with at least one crossing longer than 70 km. (3) The founding groups were small: genomes from Ranis and Zlatý kůň imply an effective population of about 300 around 45,000 years ago. (4) As they spread, they met and interbred with archaic humans: one extended period of Neanderthal gene flow, about 50,500–43,500 years ago, shared by all non-Africans, after which harmful Neanderthal variants were quickly lost; and later Denisovan admixture, about 44,000 years ago, in the ancestors of Papuans and Aboriginal Australians. (5) Populations then diverged regionally: European and East Asian ancestors split about 42,000 years ago (29,000–55,000) in the Malaspinas model, and Papuan and Aboriginal Australian ancestors about 37,000 years ago. Absolute genetic dates rest on assumed mutation rates; pedigree-based rates roughly double divergence dates compared with older phylogenetic rates.
why_it_matters: This dispersal produced the ancestors of nearly every person whose family history lies outside Africa, so the population history of Asia, Australia, the Pacific, Europe and the Americas begins with it. It also explains part of the shape of human genetic variation: people outside Africa carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA from one shared period of interbreeding, with variants that still affect immune function, skin pigmentation and metabolism, and Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry about 4% Denisovan ancestry. The settlement of Sahul by about 50,000 years ago, and possibly earlier, required repeated open-sea crossings of Wallacea, evidence that seafaring was within the reach of Pleistocene foragers. The event matters too as a test case for how science dates the deep past, because genetic clocks, radiocarbon, luminescence and fossils must all be reconciled, and the Madjedbebe debate shows how much the answer depends on the method. The counterfactual is visible in the record itself: earlier groups of Homo sapiens reached the Levant and possibly Greece more than 100,000 years before, but they did not become the main ancestors of living people. Had the later dispersal faded out as the earlier ones did, Eurasia would have remained, for longer at least, the domain of Neanderthals, Denisovans and other archaic humans, and the ancestry of most living people would be very different.

related.because: The dispersing population descended from Homo sapiens that had evolved in Africa, and its members carried the African ancestry that all non-Africans share.

perspectives.holder: Southern-route models: many mtDNA studies and coastal 'beachcomber' serial-bottleneck models, as reviewed by López et al. (2015)
perspectives.account: The main dispersal left the Horn of Africa across the Bab el-Mandeb into southern Arabia and moved along the coasts toward South Asia; Groucutt and others reply that mtDNA lineage geography alone cannot settle the route.

perspectives.holder: Pagani et al. (2015), from 225 Egyptian and Ethiopian genomes
perspectives.account: Non-African haplotypes are closer to Egyptian than to Ethiopian ones, and Egyptians split from non-Africans later (~55 kya) than Ethiopians (~65 kya), favouring a predominantly northern exit through Egypt and Sinai.

perspectives.holder: Early-and-multiple dispersal models: Groucutt et al. (2015); Hershkovitz et al. (2018) for Misliya; Harvati et al. (2019) for Apidima
perspectives.account: Homo sapiens left Africa repeatedly from at least 177,000–194,000 years ago, during humid windows, and the later successful expansion largely swamped earlier ones; Apidima 1 (>210 ka) is offered as evidence of multiple dispersals.

perspectives.holder: Critics of the Apidima 1 date and attribution, reported in 2019 coverage
perspectives.account: Raw U-series results spread over a wide range and the fragment may be considerably younger than 210,000 years; co-author Rainer Grün replied that the younger samples differ chemically from the skull.

perspectives.holder: Late single-dispersal view: O'Connell et al. (2018); supported for population structure by Sümer et al. (2024) and Malaspinas et al. (2016)
perspectives.account: The successful dispersal was a single movement about 50,000–55,000 years ago; Homo sapiens remains older than about 50,000 years outside Africa belong to other populations, and Malaspinas found a single exit supported once archaic admixture is modelled, though modern genomes alone also fit two waves.
Artefacts in primary context, with refits and optical dates, show people at Madjedbebe from around 65,000 years ago, setting a new minimum age for the dispersal out of Africa.
Artefacts likely moved down through the sand sheet by termites, rain-splash and creep, so the optical dates overstate their age; Sahul was first colonised around 48,000–50,000 years ago.

perspectives.holder: Westaway et al. (2017) versus O'Connell et al. (2018) on Lida Ajer
perspectives.account: Westaway's team dates modern human teeth in Sumatra to 73,000–63,000 years ago; O'Connell's team accepts this as the strongest pre-50 ka case but questions where the teeth originally lay in the deposit.

importance.justification: The dispersal that gave rise to nearly all human ancestry outside Africa underlies the population history of every inhabited continent, so it must be visible at whole-planet view.
